title_original: Mari Katayama Takes Root at Paris Photo

blocks.text: Sewn limbs in place of flesh, mirrors that multiply an amputated body into infinite regress: in “tree of life,” her new cycle of self-portraits, Japanese artist Mari Katayama stages herself as a world-tree. Parisian gallery Suzanne Tarasieve unveils these works at the Grand Palais, at Paris Photo.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Mari Katayama.

blocks.caption: © Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris

blocks.text: Dressed in a flesh-toned lace bodysuit, a woman holds court at the center of a mirrored chamber, the cable release of her camera gripped in her hand. Around her, hand-stitched fabric arms proliferate alongside strings of lights and organza veils threaded with hair; her lace-clad legs end in crocodile heads. “ The mirror space dissolves the boundary between ceiling and floor, ” Katayama confides, “ multiplying the body to infinity until one can no longer tell clearly which image is real and which is reflection. ”

blocks.caption: © Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris
© Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris

blocks.text: Born in 1987, the artist grew up in Gunma, northwest of Tokyo. Afflicted with tibial hemimelia — a rare condition that prevented her legs from developing — she chose, at age nine, to have both amputated. Taught to sew by her grandmother, she spent her adolescence concealing her difference; at sixteen, she reversed course, making her body the raw material of her work. Since 2011, her High Heel Project has seen her sing and model on stage, balanced on high heels fitted to her prosthetic legs, in the name of what she calls “ freedom of choice. ”

blocks.caption: © Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris
© Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris

blocks.text: A sea change arrives with tree of life . Earlier series dressed her in shells and unfurled her arms as tentacles along the beaches of Naoshima island; here, salt water gives way to sap. Bodies rise as “ monumental caryatids ” — those ancient columns carved in the form of women — while suspended textile organs, christened koilia , receive “ beings and events. ” And always, the same sovereign gesture: “ Sewing. Pressing the shutter myself. Singing. Letting go. ”

blocks.caption: © Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris
© Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris

blocks.text: The art world had long since made up its mind: unveiled at the Venice Biennale in 2019, exhibited at the MEP in 2021, celebrated at the Rencontres d’Arles in 2024, Katayama’s work has taken root in the collections of MoMA and the Tate Modern. At the Grand Palais, the gallery presents hand-printed chromogenic prints and unique frames decorated by the artist’s own hand — works commissioned by the V&A Parasol Foundation Women in Photography Project. In Ovid, Daphne turned to laurel to escape a god. Katayama reaches in the opposite direction: “The body gains strength when it is connected to others.”

blocks.caption: © Mari Katayama / Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve, Paris

blocks.text: “tree of life,” by Mari Katayama, is presented by Galerie Suzanne Tarasieve at Paris Photo , Grand Palais, Main sector, through November 15, 2026. All photographs: © Mari Katayama.
